title: The Wizard Who Wasn't Magic
blurb: Six wizard stories, from a starry hat and a lost pair of glasses to the old idea hiding under the pointed hat: that a wizard was once just a person wise enough to pay attention.

blocks.prompt: Wizard Pim and the Missing Glasses
blocks.text: Old Wizard Pim lived in a tower by the sea. Every morning he climbed the stairs to feed his owl. The owl carried letters for people far away. Pim had a long white beard and a hat full of stars. When he waved his wand, small blue sparks danced in the air. But one day Pim could not find his glasses. He looked under his book. He looked in his boot. At last the owl pointed with one wing. The glasses were sitting on top of Pim's own head. Pim laughed and gave the owl a treat.

blocks.prompt: The Spell That Found Its Day
blocks.text: Mira wanted to be a wizard more than anything. The trouble was that her spells never worked the way the book promised. When she tried to light a candle, she made it rain instead. When she tried to warm the soup, she turned it blue. Her teacher, old Master Bram, did not seem worried. One cold night the whole village lost its fire. The wood was too wet to burn. Mira stepped forward and tried her candle spell one more time. Rain poured from her hands, just as it always did. But this rain was warm, and where it fell the wet wood began to steam and then to glow. Soon every hearth in the village was lit. Master Bram smiled. A spell is not wrong, he said, just because it does something you did not expect. Sometimes the trick is finding the day it fits.

blocks.prompt: The Wand That Did Nothing
blocks.text: Every apprentice at the Tower learned the same first lesson: a wizard's power is not in the wand. Toma did not believe it. He was sure the older students kept the real secret to themselves, and that a better wand would finally make his spells hold steady. So on the night of the harvest fair, he traded his savings for a wand of black river oak, carved with silver thread. It was the most beautiful thing he had ever owned. The next morning he stood in the practice yard and raised it high. He spoke the words for a floating light, the very first spell every student learns. Nothing happened. He tried again, louder. Still nothing. The beautiful wand lay dead in his hand. Master Sable watched from the doorway. She did not laugh. She handed Toma a plain stick of pine, no thicker than a finger, and told him to try once more. This time he was too tired to expect anything. He simply pictured the light, clearly and calmly, and asked it to come. A small gold flame rose from the tip of the pine and hung in the air like a tiny sun. The wand did nothing for you, Sable said, because it had nothing to give. What holds a spell steady is a steady mind. A wand only points the way your attention is already going. Toma looked at the plain pine stick and, for the first time, understood the lesson he had been told on his very first day.

blocks.prompt: The Wizard of Harrow
blocks.text: The village of Harrow had kept a wizard for as long as anyone could remember. The wizard's job was not to throw fire or turn enemies to stone, whatever the old songs claimed. The job was quieter and harder than that. When the river rose, the wizard read the water and told the farmers which fields to abandon. When fever came, the wizard knew which weeds to boil and which to burn. When two families quarreled over a boundary stone, the wizard was the one voice both sides would still listen to. Nessa became Harrow's wizard at nineteen, younger than any before her. She had studied for six years under old Corvin, and she knew every remedy in his cracked leather book. What she did not have was the thing the villagers trusted most, which was gray hair. The first winter, a farmer named Holt refused her advice about a sick flock, certain that a girl could not know better than he did. Half his sheep died. He did not apologize, but the next spring he came to her door before planting, cap in hand, and asked what she thought. Nessa learned something that year that Corvin had never written down. A wizard's real power was not in the spells at all. It was in being trusted, and trust could not be inherited with the title. It had to be earned one hard, patient season at a time. The book gave her knowledge. Only the years would give her authority. By the time Nessa was old, with gray hair of her own at last, the village had stopped questioning her. New children assumed she had always been wise, the way children do. She let them think it. But she kept Holt's story, and told it to her own apprentice on the girl's first day. The magic that matters, she said, is slow. Do not expect the village to believe in you because of what you know. They will believe in you because of what you have done, and that takes longer than any spell in this book.

6.title: The Wizard Who Wasn't Magic
6.subtitle: A reading sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: The word wizard comes from wys, an Old English root for wise
By the 1400s it meant a sage or philosopher
Merlin, from the Arthurian legends, is the archetypal story wizard
Europe's cunning folk really sold cures, charms, and advice
The starry pointed hat draws on old images of astronomers and magi
A book of magical spells is called a grimoire

blocks.prompt: The Oldest Magic
blocks.text: There is a question every wizard's apprentice asks eventually, usually late at night, usually after a spell has failed for the tenth time: what is magic, really? Master Ines had a habit of answering questions with other questions, but this one she answered plainly, and only once. Kael had been her student for four years when he finally asked it. They were sitting in the tower's cold observatory, charting the winter stars, and he was tired enough to be honest. He said he had begun to suspect there was no such thing as magic at all, that everything they did could be explained by patience, herbs, and paying close attention. He expected her to be angry. Instead she looked pleased, the way a teacher looks when a student has finally noticed the trap in a problem. You are almost right, Ines said. Then she told him the truth she had been waiting four years to tell. Long ago, she explained, the first wizards were simply the people who paid attention when everyone else was too busy surviving. They noticed that certain leaves brought down a fever, that the river always flooded three days after a particular wind, that a sick child often needed a calm adult more than a potion. They wrote these observations down and guarded them, because knowledge was rare and rareness was power. To the frightened people around them, a person who could predict a flood or break a fever might as well have commanded the sky. The word for such a person became wizard, from an old word meaning wise. The pointed hat and the muttered spells came later, added by storytellers who found the plain truth too dull. So there is no magic, Kael said, disappointed. Ines shook her head. That is the wrong lesson, she said. There is no trick that breaks the laws of the world. But look at what these people actually did. They chose to notice. They chose to remember, to write it down, to pass it on to a stranger who would live after they were dead. Most people never bother. That choice, made over and over across a hundred lifetimes, is the closest thing to magic that has ever existed, and it is completely real. You are not learning to cheat the world, Kael. You are learning to see it clearly, and then to hand what you see to someone who has not been born yet. Kael did not answer for a long time. Above them the winter stars turned, exactly as the charts predicted they would, which had once seemed like sorcery and now seemed like something better. Years later, when Kael was the master and had his own tired, doubting apprentice, he did not answer the question with a question. He answered it plainly, and only once, the way it had been answered for him, so that the oldest magic, the handing on, would not stop with him.

(there is no rule-breaking trick, but choosing to notice, record, and hand knowledge on across lifetimes is real and rare)
(the repeated frame shows the tradition continuing through Kael; it makes the ending feel like proof of the theme, the handing on of knowledge)
(sentence: That choice, made over and over across a hundred lifetimes, is the closest thing to magic that has ever existed; it reframes magic as human effort rather than supernatural power)
